title: Corporate mentions of Trump's tariffs spiked in spring 2025
gist: PIIE text-mined 920 earnings calls from 150 S&P 500/400/600 companies and found tariff mentions collapsed from 85 percent of calls in Q2 2025 (post-Liberation Day) to 34 percent in Q2 2026, with average tariff passages per call falling from six to one. The authors read this as habituation rather than resolution — mentions peaked in every sector and were similar across market caps — and warn that if Trump reads quieter corporate pushback as acquiescence he may escalate tariffs again.

themes.theme: Tariff attention decay in earnings calls

insights.claim: In a PIIE sample of 920 earnings calls from 150 companies (January 2025 through July 2026), 85 percent of calls mentioned tariffs in Q2 2025 but only 34 percent did in Q2 2026, a collapse in corporate attention to US tariff policy.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Tariff commentary has become a fading earnings-call theme, so tariff headlines are less likely to reshape guidance narratives than in 2025 — but it also means positioning is thin if a new shock lands.
insights.quote: We found that executives in 85 percent of calls in the sample mentioned tariffs during the second quarter of 2025, peaking in the wake of Trump's Liberation Day announcement.

insights.claim: The average number of tariff-mentioning passages per earnings call fell from six in Q2 2025 to one in Q2 2026, a six-fold drop in the intensity of corporate tariff discussion.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Intensity, not just incidence, has normalized — a usable text-based gauge to track quarterly as a proxy for corporate trade-policy stress.
insights.quote: the average number of passages mentioning tariffs per earnings call dropped from six in the second quarter of 2025 to one in the second quarter of 2026

insights.claim: PIIE reads the decline in corporate tariff talk as evidence that firms now find White House tariff policy less shocking than a year earlier, not as evidence that tariffs matter less economically.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Habituation, not resolution — the tariff cost base is still in P&Ls even though managements have stopped narrating it, so tariff drag can be underestimated by narrative-driven screens.
insights.quote: These results suggest that firms find White House tariff policy less shocking now than a year ago.

insights.claim: PIIE offers three competing explanations for falling corporate tariff commentary: firms accepted tariffs as the new norm and adapted, they grew less concerned about tariff effects on their businesses, or they concluded silence was the safest way to handle a politically charged topic.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: The 'silence is strategic' channel means falling disclosure is not clean evidence of falling exposure — read gross margin and COGS detail rather than management commentary to size tariff impact.
insights.quote: Some may have decided that silence was the best way to navigate a politically charged topic.

insights.claim: The authors explicitly caveat that the observed decline in tariff mentions cannot be interpreted with certainty, keeping the finding descriptive rather than causal.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Treat the mention-count series as a sentiment indicator with unresolved identification, not as a measure of realized tariff cost.
insights.quote: While it's impossible to interpret this pattern with certainty, it could reflect several shifts in the way executives viewed Trump's tariffs.

insights.claim: Industrials, materials, and consumer discretionary executives mentioned tariffs most often, consistent with those sectors' dependence on physical goods, while communication services, utilities, and real estate mentioned them least.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Goods-heavy sectors remain the cleanest expression of tariff risk; service sectors are the natural relative-value hedge against a renewed tariff shock.
insights.locator: Mentions of tariffs by corporate leaders varied by sector

insights.claim: The Q2 2025 peak in tariff mentions showed up conspicuously in every sector, indicating the Liberation Day tariff shock was economy-wide rather than confined to goods-exposed industries.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: A tariff shock transmits as a broad market-level risk event, so index-level hedges — not just sector baskets — are the right instrument when escalation looks likely.
insights.quote: But mentions of tariffs in every sector conspicuously peaked in the second quarter of 2025.

insights.claim: Contrary to the expectation that small caps would worry more about tariffs because they lack supplier bargaining power and exemption-lobbying clout, S&P 500, MidCap 400, and SmallCap 600 companies discussed tariffs in similar patterns.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Undercuts the common long-large-cap/short-small-cap tariff trade premised on differential exemption access — at least at the level of managerial attention.
insights.quote: One might expect that smaller market cap companies would worry more about tariffs, given their weaker power to negotiate with suppliers and seek exemptions (which larger companies have successfully lobbied for).

insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Exemption access is a durable, under-modeled competitive moat for mega-caps in goods sectors if tariff rates ratchet higher.

insights.claim: The Supreme Court struck down Trump's so-called reciprocal tariffs as unconstitutional in February; he responded with temporary tariffs that expired on July 24 and, the same day, ordered new tariffs he said would combat forced labor.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Legal defeat has not reduced tariff coverage — the administration substitutes new authorities, so betting on courts to unwind tariff exposure has repeatedly failed.
insights.quote: He followed that ruling by announcing temporary tariffs that expired on July 24, the same day he ordered new tariffs that he said would combat forced labor.

insights.claim: US trade policy in Trump's second term has imposed successive waves of new tariffs on nearly all imports from almost all countries, surprising firms, financial markets, and governments alike.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Near-universal coverage makes tariff risk a macro factor rather than an idiosyncratic supply-chain issue for a handful of importers.
insights.quote: He has surprised firms, financial markets, and governments by imposing successive waves of new tariffs on nearly all imports from almost all countries.

insights.claim: RPM International chair Frank Sullivan told a July 22, 2026 earnings call that the year ahead would likely be another volatile one because the administration seems not to like stability — an unusually blunt executive characterization of US tariff policy risk.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Goods-producing managements still plan for volatility even as aggregate tariff commentary fades — guidance in coatings and chemicals carries wider-than-normal error bars.
insights.quote: Our guess is it's going to be another volatile year. We have an administration that seems to not like stability.

insights.claim: PIIE warns that if Trump interprets declining corporate pushback on tariffs as acquiescence, he could raise tariffs further despite potential harm to businesses and consumers.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Corporate silence is itself a risk factor — the quieter earnings calls get on tariffs, the higher the odds of the next escalation, an inverted contrarian signal.
insights.quote: If he sees declining corporate pushback as acquiescence, he could choose to raise tariffs further, despite potential harms to businesses and consumers.
insights.locator: Trump may deliver new tariff shocks

insights.claim: A renewed US tariff shock should sharply increase tariff mentions in future earnings calls, making the mention-count series a testable real-time indicator of policy shock severity.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Build or buy an earnings-call keyword tracker: a re-spike in tariff passages per call would flag a regime change before it shows up in reported margins.
insights.quote: Such a scenario should sharply increase mention of tariffs in future earnings calls.
insights.locator: Trump may deliver new tariff shocks

insights.claim: The PIIE tariff-mention count excludes analyst questions during earnings-call Q&A because they reflect sell-side rather than company sentiment, but it does count management answers to those questions.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: The series measures management-voiced concern specifically, so it is a cleaner read on corporate framing than on investor anxiety about tariffs.
insights.locator: Notes 1. Questions raised during earnings calls

insights.claim: The authors concede that counting 'passages' containing the word tariff is an arbitrary unit, and report that a robustness check using total 'tariff' word counts per call produced similar results.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: The measured decline in tariff attention is robust to the counting choice, which strengthens the case for using it as a tracked indicator.
insights.quote: A robustness check was run using total "tariff" word counts per call, with similar results.
